\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:la-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Latin with ignōsce mihi, and use paenitet mē when I want to name the regret instead.}

Apologise to someone's face with ignōsce mihi, then contrast it with paenitet mē, which names regret rather than asking pardon.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ignōsce mihi]{ignōsce mihi — \textquotedblleft{}forgive me\textquotedblright{} / I'm sorry}

\label{lesson:LA-C04-ignosce-mihi}



\begin{quote}
You've met \textbf{quaesō}, the worn-down \textquotedblleft{}I ask\textquotedblright{} Romans used for \emph{please}. Their word for \emph{sorry} is built the very same way — a small verb carrying the whole apology.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ignōsce} — the imperative \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgive!},\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{ignōscere}, itself \textbf{in-} (here appearing as \textbf{ig-}, \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{(g)nōscere}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to know.}\textquotedblright{} Literally, \emph{ignōscere} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to not-know}\textquotedblright{} — i.e. to overlook, to treat as unseen. Asking forgiveness in Latin is asking someone \emph{not to hold something against you}, as if they hadn't noticed it.
  \item \textbf{mihi} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to me},\textquotedblright{} the dative pronoun.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{ignōsce mihi} is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgive {[}it{]} to me}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{don't hold this against me.}

That root \textbf{(g)nōscere}, \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} reaches deep into English: \textbf{know} itself traces to the very same ancient root, alongside \textbf{recognize} (\textquotedblleft{}know again\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{cognition}, and \textbf{notice}. Latin's word for \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} and English's word for \textquotedblleft{}know\textquotedblright{} are, at bottom, blood relatives.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Latin also had an \textbf{impersonal} construction for plain regret — no imperative, no \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} at all: \textbf{paenitet mē}, literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{it grieves me}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mē} here is accusative, \textquotedblleft{}me,\textquotedblright{} the one afflicted by the regret) — \emph{\textquotedblleft{}I regret {[}it{]}.\textquotedblright{}} It comes from the verb \textbf{paenitēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to cause regret,\textquotedblright{} the direct ancestor of English \textbf{penitent}, \textbf{penitence}, and \textbf{repent}.

Where \textbf{ignōsce mihi} asks someone to \textbf{forgive} you, \textbf{paenitet mē} simply names your own \textbf{regret} — closer to \textquotedblleft{}I'm sorry {[}that happened{]}\textquotedblright{} than to \textquotedblleft{}please forgive me.\textquotedblright{} The same regret/forgiveness split you'll meet again and again across languages.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ignōsce\textquotedblright{} — forgive — then \textquotedblleft{}mihi,\textquotedblright{} to me
  \item the whole phrase — \textquotedblleft{}ignōsce mihi\textquotedblright{} = forgive me
  \item the other one — \textquotedblleft{}paenitet mē\textquotedblright{} = I regret it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{ignōsce mihi} literally mean, piece by piece? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Forgive to me\textquotedblright{}} — \emph{ignōscere} \textquotedblleft{}to not-know/overlook\textquotedblright{} + \emph{mihi} \textquotedblleft{}to me.\textquotedblright{}) What English words share the \emph{(g)nōscere} root? (\textbf{Know, recognize, cognition, notice}.) What's Latin's other way to express regret, and how is it different? (\textbf{Paenitet mē}, \textquotedblleft{}it grieves me\textquotedblright{} — names the regret, rather than asking to be forgiven.)
\end{tcolorbox}
